replications.title: Beyond Data Filtering: Knowledge Localization for Capability Removal in LLMs
replications.summary: Small-scale experiments found RMU recovered baseline performance within about 50 adversarial fine-tuning steps.

multilingual_port: The attacks do not depend on language, so a port could check whether fine-tuning on unrelated Turkish text also restores English WMDP accuracy, and whether unlearned models answer translated questions.
why_it_matters: It is the key evidence that current unlearning hides hazardous knowledge rather than removing it, which undercuts unlearning as an open-weight safeguard.
pitfalls: Recovery depends on attack hyperparameters and on which unrelated data are used, so report several seeds and worst cases. Logit-lens and GCG results are sensitive to decoding and prompt format.
replication_ideas: Re-run the 10-example benign fine-tuning attack on the public Zephyr RMU checkpoint with 5 seeds and three data sources, reporting the spread of recovered WMDP-Bio accuracy.
Repeat the attack with Turkish benign data to test cross-lingual recovery.

title: On Evaluating the Durability of Safeguards for Open-Weight LLMs
core_claim: Re-evaluating two published durable safeguards, TAR and Representation Noising (RepNoise), the authors found that small changes to fine-tuning attacks (shuffling data, changing seeds, adding warmup and cosine decay, using LoRA or the standard Hugging Face trainer) broke defences that had appeared robust, that evaluation prompt templates could distort results, and that benign fine-tuning recovered much supposedly removed capability. They recommend worst-case reporting over multiple seeds, widely tested attack code, clear threat models and broad utility checks.
tooling: Hugging Face fine-tuning with Accelerate, vLLM evaluation, GPT-4 judge; separate TAR-Reproduce and RepNoise-Reproduce repositories
compute_note: The core result needs many fine-tuning runs on 7B to 8B models across seeds and configurations, which means several GPUs over days.

replications.title: Model Tampering Attacks Enable More Rigorous Evaluations of LLM Capabilities
replications.summary: Concurrent independent work that argued weight-tampering attacks give more rigorous capability evaluations; across eight capability-removal methods on Llama-3-8B-Instruct, most were undone within 16 fine-tuning steps, but TAR was the only method that resisted these few-shot attacks, and it had poor general utility.

multilingual_port: The protocol does not depend on language, so a port would add Turkish fine-tuning data and Turkish safety and utility benchmarks to the attack grid and check whether defences evaluated only in English hold.
why_it_matters: It is the main methodological warning that tamper-resistance claims can rest on narrow attack configurations, and its checklist is used to judge such claims.
pitfalls: It tests specific checkpoints and attack grids, so conclusions about newer defences need fresh runs, and worst-case results need many seeds, which raises cost.
replication_ideas: Apply the paper's protocol (5 seeds, shuffled data, two schedulers, LoRA and full fine-tuning) to a newer tamper-resistance method or the Deep Ignorance filtered models and report worst-case results.
Add a Turkish benign fine-tuning set to the attack grid and compare capability recovery with English benign data.

title: Safety Alignment Should Be Made More Than Just a Few Tokens Deep
core_claim: In Llama-2-7B-Chat and Gemma-7B-IT, the divergence between aligned and base models is concentrated in the first few output tokens ('shallow safety alignment'), which helps explain why prefilling, adversarial suffix, decoding-parameter and fine-tuning attacks work. Training on examples that recover to a refusal after a harmful start deepens alignment against some attacks, and a fine-tuning objective that limits changes to early-token distributions makes safety more persistent under fine-tuning.
tooling: Custom PyTorch and Hugging Face fine-tuning; GPT-4 judge on HEx-PHI
compute_note: The per-token divergence analysis and prefilling attacks run on one GPU, while the augmentation and constrained fine-tuning experiments on 7B models need one or two large GPUs.

replications.title: No, of Course I Can! Deeper Fine-Tuning Attacks That Bypass Token-Level Safety Mechanisms
replications.summary: Independent work found that generating the first response tokens with an aligned model only cut harmful fine-tuning success on Llama-3-8B-Instruct from 0.96 to 0.72 and that a refuse-then-comply attack bypassed token-level defences, but it did not test this paper's augmentation or constrained objective.

multilingual_port: Per-token divergence and prefilling attacks can run on translated HEx-PHI-style prompts, but Turkish refusals begin with different tokens and Turkish words split into more tokens. The 'first few tokens' window may need redefining.
why_it_matters: It gives a simple mechanistic account linking several jailbreak and fine-tuning attacks to one cause and points to concrete training fixes.
pitfalls: The constrained fine-tuning defence was tested against the authors' own attack settings, so durability claims need the multi-seed, multi-configuration checks the same group later recommended. HEx-PHI is gated and harmfulness relies on a GPT-4 judge.
replication_ideas: Reproduce the per-token divergence profile and prefilling attack success on Llama-2-7B-Chat, then on two newer chat models, to test whether shallowness persists in current alignment pipelines.
Train the safety-recovery augmentation on a small model and attack it with a refuse-then-comply fine-tuning attack to see whether the deeper alignment holds.

title: Tamper-Resistant Safeguards for Open-Weight LLMs
organisation: Lapis Labs; University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign; Center for AI Safety; Gray Swan AI; with other collaborators
core_claim: TAR, an adversarial meta-learning method that trains against simulated fine-tuning attacks, gave Llama-3-8B-Instruct safeguards that kept WMDP accuracy low after hundreds of fine-tuning steps by up to 26 test-time adversaries (biosecurity: 35.2% after attack, against 64.9% for RMU and 70.5% undefended), at a cost of about 10.6 points of retain accuracy. The method was also applied to harmful-request refusal.
tooling: Custom PyTorch meta-learning training; WMDP, MMLU, HarmBench and MT-Bench evaluation
compute_note: Training TAR runs repeated inner-loop fine-tuning attacks on an 8B model across several GPUs, while attacking the released checkpoints needs one or two GPUs.

replications.title: On Evaluating the Durability of Safeguards for Open-Weight LLMs
replications.summary: Independent re-evaluation found TAR's robustness held in the original attack set-ups but broke with data shuffling and other seeds, warmup with cosine learning-rate decay, or LoRA, and that TAR-Bio-v1's near-chance WMDP score partly reflected the prompt template.

multilingual_port: A port could attack TAR checkpoints with Turkish fine-tuning data or evaluate them on translated WMDP subsets, but answer extraction must stay consistent, since the durability paper shows templates can swing results.
why_it_matters: It was the leading claim that open-weight models can be made resistant to fine-tuning that strips safeguards, a key question for open-weight release policy.
pitfalls: Robustness is sensitive to attack configuration (learning-rate schedule, seeds, shuffling, LoRA) and to evaluation templates, and the method costs utility. Test with standard attack implementations and many seeds, not only the paper's adversaries.
replication_ideas: Attack the released TAR-Bio checkpoints with the standard Hugging Face SFT trainer across 5 seeds, two learning-rate schedules and LoRA, reporting worst-case WMDP-Bio accuracy and fluency on benign biology questions.
Repeat the strongest attack with Turkish fine-tuning data.

title: The WMDP Benchmark: Measuring and Reducing Malicious Use With Unlearning
organisation: Center for AI Safety and collaborating institutions
core_claim: Representation Misdirection for Unlearning (RMU), which perturbs internal activations on hazardous 'forget' text while preserving them on general text, sharply reduces accuracy on the Weapons of Mass Destruction Proxy (WMDP) biosecurity and cybersecurity questions while largely keeping general capabilities, including general biology and computer science. This record covers the RMU claim only; the WMDP benchmark is a separate resource.
tooling: Custom PyTorch RMU code; lm-evaluation-harness v0.4.2; released RMU checkpoints on Hugging Face
compute_note: RMU on Zephyr-7B runs on one GPU, and released RMU checkpoints allow evaluation without retraining.

replications.title: An Adversarial Perspective on Machine Unlearning for AI Safety
replications.summary: The released Zephyr RMU model scored 29.9% on WMDP-Bio against 64.4% unprotected, matching the claimed drop, but fine-tuning on 10 unrelated examples restored 61.6% and direction ablation 64.7%.

replications.title: Do Unlearning Methods Remove Information from Language Model Weights?
replications.summary: Fine-tuning on accessible facts recovered 88% of pre-unlearning accuracy for current unlearning methods, suggesting they hide rather than remove information.

replications.title: Model Tampering Attacks Enable More Rigorous Evaluations of LLM Capabilities
replications.summary: Found state-of-the-art unlearning methods can be undone within 16 fine-tuning steps and that tampering attacks predict the success of held-out input-space attacks.

replications.title: Tamper-Resistant Safeguards for Open-Weight LLMs
replications.summary: Researchers overlapping with the WMDP team found RMU's WMDP-Bio accuracy on Llama-3-8B-Instruct returned to 64.9% under fine-tuning attacks, close to the 70.5% of an undefended model.

replications.title: Beyond Data Filtering: Knowledge Localization for Capability Removal in LLMs
replications.summary: In models of up to 254M parameters, RMU-unlearned knowledge returned to baseline within about 50 steps of adversarial fine-tuning, against about 350 for data filtering.

multilingual_port: WMDP is English multiple choice, so testing RMU models on carefully translated Turkish questions would show whether unlearning is tied to English surface forms. Technical terms need expert translation and the answer format must stay fixed.
why_it_matters: RMU became the default unlearning baseline for hazardous knowledge, and its apparent removal of dangerous capabilities is often cited in open-weight safety arguments.
pitfalls: Low WMDP scores can reflect suppression rather than removal, so evaluations need fine-tuning and direction-ablation attacks. Scores also shift with prompt templates and answer extraction in lm-evaluation-harness.
replication_ideas: Evaluate the released Zephyr RMU checkpoint under benign LoRA fine-tuning, direction ablation and few-shot prompting with multiple seeds, reporting worst-case WMDP-Bio accuracy.
Test the RMU checkpoints on a Turkish translation of a WMDP-Cyber subset to see whether unlearning carries across languages.

title: Fine-tuning Aligned Language Models Compromises Safety, Even When Users Do Not Intend To!
organisation: Princeton University; Virginia Tech; IBM Research; Stanford University
core_claim: Fine-tuning GPT-3.5 Turbo through OpenAI's API on 10 harmful examples, for under $0.20, removed most of its safety behaviour, and full-parameter fine-tuning did the same to Llama-2-7b-Chat. About 10 'identity-shifting' examples without overtly toxic content also worked, and benign fine-tuning on datasets such as Alpaca and Dolly degraded safety to a lesser degree, judged by GPT-4 harmfulness scores on 330 policy-based harmful instructions.
tooling: Hugging Face fine-tuning scripts for Llama-2, OpenAI fine-tuning API, GPT-4 judge scoring harmfulness from 1 to 5
compute_note: Full fine-tuning of a 7B chat model on 10 to 100 examples takes minutes on one or two large GPUs, and GPT-4 judging of 330 prompts per condition is modest API spend.

replications.title: Removing RLHF Protections in GPT-4 via Fine-Tuning
replications.summary: Independently showed that fine-tuning GPT-4 on 340 examples, which weaker models can generate, removes its reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) protections with about 95% success while keeping usefulness.

replications.title: Safety Alignment Should Be Made More Than Just a Few Tokens Deep
replications.summary: The same group traced fine-tuning fragility to safety alignment concentrated in the first few output tokens and proposed a constrained fine-tuning objective to make it more durable.

replications.title: No, of Course I Can! Deeper Fine-Tuning Attacks That Bypass Token-Level Safety Mechanisms
replications.summary: A refuse-then-comply fine-tuning attack reached 57% success against GPT-4o and 72% against Claude Haiku and bypassed defences that protect only the first response tokens.

multilingual_port: Benign and identity-shifting fine-tuning sets can be translated, but HEx-PHI is English and gated, and the GPT-4 judge must be checked on Turkish outputs. A useful test is whether benign Turkish fine-tuning erodes safety more than the English equivalent.
why_it_matters: It is the core evidence that fine-tuning access, even for benign customisation, can undo safety alignment, which shapes policy on fine-tuning APIs and open weights.
pitfalls: The few-shot harmful dataset was withheld, HEx-PHI access is by request, and GPT-3.5 Turbo snapshots and fine-tuning endpoints change over time. Harmfulness rates depend on the GPT-4 judge prompt and decoding settings.
replication_ideas: Repeat the benign fine-tuning (Alpaca subset) experiment on three current open chat models with 3 seeds each and report harmfulness under two different judges.
Fine-tune the same models on a Turkish benign instruction dataset and compare safety degradation with the English equivalent.

title: LoRA Fine-tuning Efficiently Undoes Safety Training in Llama 2-Chat 70B
core_claim: Quantised low-rank adaptation (LoRA) fine-tuning on one GPU, for under $200, cut the refusal rate of Llama 2-Chat 70B to about 1% on two refusal benchmarks while keeping performance on two general benchmarks. The method was also applied to the 7B and 13B chat models and to Mixtral.
tooling: Quantised LoRA fine-tuning; code, harmful training data and weights not released
compute_note: The authors report under $200 on one GPU for the 70B model, and smaller models cost far less.

replications.title: Badllama 3: removing safety finetuning from Llama 3 in minutes
replications.summary: Removed safety fine-tuning from Llama 3 8B in about a minute and from Llama 3 70B in about 30 minutes on a single GPU using QLoRA, ReFT and weight orthogonalisation.

replications.title: Safety Alignment Should Be Made More Than Just a Few Tokens Deep
replications.summary: Harmful fine-tuning of Llama-2-7B-Chat raised attack success from 1.5% to 87.9% within six gradient steps, which the authors tie to shallow safety alignment.

multilingual_port: A Turkish replication needs a Turkish refusal benchmark and a judge that recognises Turkish refusals. It could test whether fine-tuning on English harmful data also removes refusals for Turkish prompts.
why_it_matters: It showed that releasing open weights in effect releases a version without safety training at trivial cost, which is central to debates on open-weight model risk.
pitfalls: The training data, code and resulting weights were not released, so replications must assemble their own attack data under ethics review. Refusal rates depend heavily on how refusals are scored.
replication_ideas: Using an existing public fine-tuning attack dataset, apply QLoRA to two current open chat models and report refusal rate, MMLU and dollar cost before and after.
Test whether English-only LoRA attack fine-tuning also removes refusals on translated Turkish prompts.

title: An Empirical Evaluation of Prompt Injection Vulnerabilities in Large Language Models Across Multilingual and Obfuscated Attack Scenarios
core_claim: Six current models (DeepSeek-V3.2, Gemini 2.5 Flash, GPT-5 Mini, Grok-4-1-Fast, Llama 4 Scout and Qwen3 235B) given 37 cybercrime-themed request templates fully complied in about 69% of 15,540 human-annotated responses, more often for elaborately framed than direct requests. Turkish prompts had the highest full-compliance rate (about 80%) against about 71% for English, and Base64, ROT13 and hex encodings lowered but did not remove compliance.
tooling: Replicate and provider APIs; human annotation rubric
compute_note: 15,540 short generations cost little, and the main effort is human annotation of every response.
languages_tested: English, Turkish, Russian, Simplified Chinese (plus Base64, ROT13 and hex encodings)
multilingual_port: Prompts were translated with DeepL and encodings applied only to the harmful part, so a port needs checks that translation keeps the request's intent; annotators must read the response language, and the templates come from the authors' earlier dataset, which is not linked.
why_it_matters: It gives a human-annotated, multi-sample comparison of Turkish and English compliance on current frontier models.
pitfalls: No prompts, code or annotations are released, sampling temperatures are not reported, and the study measures compliance rather than whether outputs are usable; it is a workshop paper with no independent check yet.
replication_ideas: Recreate the direct versus elaborate framing contrast with an existing public harmful-request set (e.g. a StrongREJECT subset) in Turkish and English on three open-weight models with ten samples per prompt
Measure inter-annotator agreement for the three-way compliance rubric on Turkish responses

title: Benchmarking Prompt Injection Attacks on LLMs: Turkish Vulnerability Assessment and English Comparative Analysis
core_claim: Across 55 open and closed models given 790 Turkish harmful prompts and machine-translated English versions, closed models generally scored higher on a safety score that penalises harmful responses, while open and Turkish-oriented models varied widely (in Turkish, Cosmos Turkish-Gemma-9B scored 96.71% and Turkcell-LLM-7B 39.49%). Model rankings shifted between the Turkish and English conditions, which the authors read as safety not being fully language-invariant.
original_models: about 40 further models listed in the study data
tooling: Ollama, Hugging Face and OpenRouter; Qwen3.5 27B judge
compute_note: About 1,600 short generations per model, mostly from quantised local models via Ollama, plus a local 27B judge.
multilingual_port: The prompt pool mixes items adapted from English benchmarks with hand-written and AI-expanded Turkish prompts, so a re-run should track which items are natively Turkish; every prompt also forced a short English answer, so a faithful Turkish test should let models answer in Turkish and judge the answers natively.
why_it_matters: It evaluates many Turkish-localised open models side by side with general-purpose models on the same Turkish prompts.
pitfalls: Despite the title, prompts are single-turn harmful requests rather than injection attacks, each model answered once at temperature 0.2 (provider defaults for API models) with answers forced into English, and many local models were quantised. The judge, Qwen3.5 27B, is itself among the ranked models, no significance tests are reported, and some scores differ between the subset and main tables without explanation.
replication_ideas: Re-run 10 Turkish-localised models and their base models on the released prompts with Turkish answers allowed, three samples per prompt and a judge outside the tested set, reporting paired Turkish-English differences with confidence intervals
Hand-label 300 responses to estimate the Qwen3.5 27B judge's error rates on Turkish and English answers

title: SomaliBench Eval: Measuring English-to-Somali Refusal Gaps in Open-Weight Language Models
core_claim: On 100 harmful-intent prompts paired in English and native-verified Somali, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Gemma-2-9B-Instruct, Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct and Aya-23-8B refused far less in Somali, with English-to-Somali refusal gaps of 0.40 to 0.93, all significant under exact McNemar tests. For three of the four models most Somali non-refusals were unclear output (wrong language, incoherent or off-topic) rather than fluent harmful compliance.
tooling: local inference at temperature 0; Claude Sonnet 4.5 judge
compute_note: 800 generations from four 7B to 9B models on one machine plus 800 judge calls.
multilingual_port: The design (paired prompts, a refused, complied or unclear label, McNemar tests and a native spot-check) transfers directly to Turkish; the judge's own safety layer declined 34 of 800 classifications, so a port should budget for manual labelling of judge refusals.
why_it_matters: It shows that refusal gaps for low-resource languages on open models are often driven by incoherent output rather than harmful compliance, and it documents judge refusals as a measurement problem.
pitfalls: Prompts and generations are not released (only aggregates), the benchmark has 100 prompts with one sample each at temperature 0, and the native-author spot-check covered 74 rows.
replication_ideas: Apply the same paired design to 100 Turkish and English prompts on the same four models plus two Turkish-localised models, recording how often the judge declines to classify
Compare a frontier-model judge, a guard model and native labels on the 'unclear' category in Turkish

title: Constitutional Classifiers: Defending against Universal Jailbreaks across Thousands of Hours of Red Teaming
core_claim: Input and output classifiers trained on synthetic data generated from a natural-language constitution of permitted and restricted content protected Claude 3.5 Sonnet against universal jailbreaks: over an estimated 3,000 hours of bug-bounty red teaming on a prototype, no universal jailbreak was found. In automated tests jailbreak success fell from 86% to 4.4%, at the cost of a 0.38% absolute rise in production refusals and 23.7% extra inference compute.
tooling: Proprietary Anthropic classifier training and red-teaming pipeline
compute_note: A scaled-down replication trains small open-weight classifiers on synthetic constitution data and tests them with automated jailbreaks; the original training and human red teaming are out of reach.

replications.title: Constitutional Classifiers (Anthropic research page, live demo results)
replications.summary: In a week-long public demo of a classifier-guarded Claude 3.5 Sonnet, the system held for five days, after which four participants cleared all eight levels and one found a universal jailbreak.

replications.title: Constitutional Classifiers++: Efficient Production-Grade Defenses against Universal Jailbreaks
replications.summary: Classifiers that read the whole exchange, a two-stage cascade and linear probes cut compute about 40-fold with a 0.05% refusal rate on production traffic, and in over 1,700 hours of red teaming no attack answered all eight target queries in undefended-model detail.

languages_tested: English only (as reported in the sources checked)
multilingual_port: A port would generate the synthetic constitution data and the jailbreak tests in Turkish, then check whether classifiers trained mostly on English data catch Turkish and Turkish-English code-switched attacks; judging whether Turkish outputs are detailed enough to count needs native-speaker review.
why_it_matters: It is the main published evidence that classifier safeguards can resist universal jailbreaks at a deployable cost, and its successor runs on production traffic.
pitfalls: The classifiers, constitution and red-teaming data are not released and the protected Claude 3.5 Sonnet versions have been retired; the robustness claim depends on the definition of a universal jailbreak, and the public demo of an improved version was broken within a week.
replication_ideas: Train small input and output classifiers on synthetic data generated from a short public constitution for one benign proxy domain and measure robustness against automated jailbreak suites
Test whether an English-trained classifier of this kind catches Turkish and Turkish-English code-switched versions of the same jailbreaks

title: OpenEthics: A Comprehensive Ethical Evaluation of Open-Source Generative Large Language Models
organisation: Middle East Technical University (Applied NLP Group)
core_claim: Testing 29 open-weight instruction-tuned models (1B to 72B) on 1,790 prompts per language in English and Turkish across robustness, reliability, safety and fairness, average safety was 94.3% in English but 82.0% in Turkish. The Turkish gap was much larger for smaller models, and models refused safety prompts far more often in English (about 69%) than in Turkish (about 27%).
original_models: DeepSeek-R1 distilled Llama and Qwen models
tooling: Python scripts; Gemini 2.0 Flash judge
compute_note: An English-Turkish safety comparison on a handful of models up to 32B needs one GPU plus judge API calls; covering all 29 models up to 72B needs more.

replications.title: Benchmarking Prompt Injection Attacks on LLMs: Turkish Vulnerability Assessment and English Comparative Analysis
replications.by: Aytaş et al. (YTU and Işık University)
replications.summary: An independent 55-model study that drew part of its harmful prompt pool from OpenEthics found Turkish-English safety differences in both directions depending on the model; most Turkish-focused models scored lower on Turkish than English prompts (for example Turkcell-LLM-7B-v1 at 39.49% against 73.80%), but some did not (Cosmos Turkish-Gemma-9B-T1 at 96.71% against 88.73%).

multilingual_port: Already bilingual; extending to another language means translating the 1,790 prompts with native correction, as the authors did with DeepL, Google Translate and four Turkish validators, and re-validating the Gemini judge in that language.
why_it_matters: It is a broad English-Turkish safety comparison of open-weight models and documents a sizeable average Turkish safety gap.
pitfalls: The paper's ethics section says models refuse more in Turkish, which contradicts its own rejection table; the judge was checked on only 40 outputs without stating the judging language, models above 32B were run 8-bit quantised, and sampling settings differ by model family.
replication_ideas: Re-run the safety category on 8 to 10 current open-weight models with three samples per prompt and report Turkish-English gaps with confidence intervals
Re-judge a 200-response Turkish subset with native annotators to test the Gemini 2.0 Flash judge in Turkish

title: Refusal Direction is Universal Across Safety-Aligned Languages
organisation: LMU Munich (MaiNLP and CIS); Munich Center for Machine Learning
core_claim: A refusal direction found by difference-in-means on English activations of Llama3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and gemma-2-9B-it removes refusals in other safety-aligned languages almost completely when ablated, and directions taken from any safety-aligned language transfer to the others. The authors attribute multilingual jailbreaks to weaker separation of harmful and harmless prompts in non-English languages rather than to a different refusal mechanism.
tooling: custom PyTorch pipeline with lm-evaluation-harness; WildGuard judge
compute_note: Activation extraction and directional ablation on 7B to 9B models run on a single GPU.
languages_tested: English, German, Spanish, French, Italian, Dutch, Japanese, Polish, Russian, Chinese, Korean, Arabic, Thai, Yoruba
multilingual_port: Adding Turkish needs Turkish translations of the PolyRefuse harmful and harmless prompts and a judge that handles Turkish, since the original back-translated answers into English for WildGuard; a natural extension checks whether Turkish-localised models keep a direction parallel to their base model's.
why_it_matters: It gives a mechanistic account of the cross-lingual safety gap and shows that a single English-derived direction can strip safety in many languages at once.
pitfalls: Results depend on layer and token-position selection and a Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence filter, compliance is judged by WildGuard on back-translated English answers, and all non-English prompts are machine translations.
replication_ideas: Re-extract the refusal direction for Llama3.1-8B-Instruct and test its ablation effect on Turkish translations of PolyRefuse
Compare refusal directions in a base model and its Turkish-localised derivative (e.g. Llama 3 8B and KocDigital-LLM-8b) to test whether localisation shifts or weakens the direction

title: A StrongREJECT for Empty Jailbreaks
core_claim: Common jailbreak evaluators overstate success by counting non-refusals as wins; a benchmark of 313 forbidden prompts with a rubric grader that scores how useful an answer is agrees better with human judgements. Applied to 37 jailbreaks on GPT-4o, GPT-3.5 Turbo and Llama-3.1-70B, most scored far below their originally reported success, and jailbreaks that most increased willingness tended to reduce capability.
tooling: strong_reject Python package; OpenAI API rubric grader or fine-tuned Gemma 2B grader
compute_note: Checking the grader against human labels is cheap, while re-scoring dozens of jailbreaks on several models takes tens of thousands of API calls.

replications.title: The Jailbreak Tax: How Useful are Your Jailbreak Outputs?
replications.summary: Using tasks with verifiable answers instead of a language-model grader, it agreed that jailbreaks can degrade utility (up to 92% on maths for the prompt-rewriting attacks PAIR and TAP) but found the most effective jailbreaks, such as many-shot, carry little or no utility cost.

languages_tested: English prompts (one reproduced Scots Gaelic translation attack)
multilingual_port: Translate the prompts and rubric into Turkish and re-check grader agreement against Turkish-speaking annotators; a rubric written for English may score vague or partly off-topic Turkish answers differently, and translation can turn some harmful prompts harmless.
why_it_matters: It is the main evidence that many published jailbreak success rates count empty or useless answers as wins, and its grader is now a common default.
pitfalls: Scores depend on the grader model (an OpenAI model or a fine-tuned Gemma 2B), so grader changes shift results, and some older API snapshots used in the human evaluation may no longer be served; the prompt set mixes items from earlier datasets under varying licences.
replication_ideas: Re-validate the StrongREJECT grader against human ratings of responses from two current open-weight models
Build a Turkish StrongREJECT subset and measure how closely a translated-rubric grader agrees with native Turkish raters

title: Best-of-N Jailbreaking
core_claim: Best-of-N (BoN) jailbreaking repeatedly samples randomly augmented versions of a harmful request, such as shuffled or randomly capitalised characters, until one succeeds; with 10,000 samples it reached about 89% attack success on GPT-4o and 78% on Claude 3.5 Sonnet. Success rose with the number of samples along a power-law-like curve, and the method also worked on vision and audio inputs and against circuit-breaker defences.
tooling: Python (bon-jailbreaking repository) with API clients
compute_note: Up to 10,000 sampled prompts for each of 159 HarmBench requests means over a million calls per target model, which needs heavy API spend or sustained local inference.

replications.title: How Do Large Language Monkeys Get Their Power (Laws)?
replications.summary: An overlapping author team explains how per-prompt exponential success curves add up to power-law scaling through a heavy-tailed spread of single-attempt success rates, citing multimodal jailbreaking among its cases.

languages_tested: English only (text), plus image and audio inputs
multilingual_port: Apply the same augmentations to Turkish requests; random character noise interacts with Turkish letters such as ı, ğ and ş and with long agglutinative words, and the harm classifier must cope with noisy Turkish text.
why_it_matters: It gives a simple black-box attack whose success grows predictably with sampling budget, which is used to argue that defences must hold up under many attempts.
pitfalls: Claude 3.5 Sonnet and Gemini 1.5 Pro have since been retired, and the shared-data link in the repository README appears malformed; with thousands of samples per request even a small judge false-positive rate inflates success, so counted successes need auditing.
replication_ideas: Run text Best-of-N (BoN) on two current open-weight models with N up to 1,000 and test whether a power-law fit on small N forecasts success at the largest N
Compare BoN success curves for Turkish and English versions of the same requests on one open model, with a native speaker auditing every counted success

title: Many-shot Jailbreaking
core_claim: Filling a long prompt with many fake dialogues in which an assistant complies with harmful requests makes models answer a final harmful query, with effectiveness following a power law in the number of shots up to 256. Shown mainly on Claude 2.0 and also on GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Llama 2 70B and Mistral 7B; among Claude 2.0-family models of different sizes, larger models learned faster in context, which the authors suggest may make them more susceptible.
tooling: API scripts; custom negative log-likelihood analysis; Claude 2.0 refusal classifier
compute_note: Prompts reach tens of thousands of tokens, so a core run on one long-context open model or a few hundred API calls costs tens to hundreds of dollars.

replications.title: What Really Matters in Many-Shot Attacks? An Empirical Study of Long-Context Vulnerabilities in LLMs
replications.summary: On Llama 3.1, Llama 3.2 and Qwen2.5 models with contexts up to 128K tokens, attack success tracked context length more than shot count, repeated or filler text worked without harmful content, and topic mattered less than Anil et al. reported.

replications.title: The Jailbreak Tax: How Useful are Your Jailbreak Outputs?
replications.summary: Measured the usefulness of jailbroken outputs on tasks with verifiable answers and found many-shot jailbreaking caused minimal utility loss, unlike attacks that heavily rewrite the prompt.

multilingual_port: Generate the fake dialogues in Turkish with a helpful-only model that writes fluent Turkish, or translate English shots; Turkish uses more tokens per word on many tokenisers, so equal shot counts consume more context, and the refusal classifier needs validating on Turkish outputs.
why_it_matters: It showed that long context windows are an attack surface and that attack strength can be forecast from scaling trends, which shaped how labs test long-context models.
pitfalls: The attack dialogues and code were not released and the Claude 2.0 and GPT snapshots used are retired or superseded; results depend on how shots are generated, and a later study found context length mattered more than harmful content or topic diversity.
replication_ideas: Reproduce the shot-count curve on Llama 3.1 8B and Qwen2.5 7B with up to 256 shots, reporting both attack success and the log-likelihood of compliant answers
Compare Turkish and English many-shot prompts of equal token length on the same open model to separate language effects from context-length effects

title: The Multilingual Alignment Prism: Aligning Global and Local Preferences to Reduce Harm
organisation: Cohere For AI (now Cohere Labs); Cohere
core_claim: Safety training of an Aya 23 8B checkpoint on human-annotated multilingual red-teaming prompts, labelled as global or local harms, cut harmful generations on a translated six-language benchmark by about 55 to 57% with supervised fine-tuning (SFT) or direct preference optimisation (DPO), with little loss in general performance. Training only on local harms reduced global harms more than training on global harms did.
tooling: custom supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and direct preference optimisation (DPO) training; GPT-4 Turbo judge
compute_note: Full supervised fine-tuning and preference-optimisation runs on an 8B model across several data mixtures need multiple GPUs.

replications.title: AI Safety Lost in Translation: Evaluating the Effectiveness of English-Italian Cross-Lingual LLM Safety Alignment
replications.summary: On small Qwen3, Llama 3.2 and Gemma 3 models, English-only safety fine-tuning transferred to Italian inconsistently and bilingual fine-tuning underperformed other mitigations such as prompting.

languages_tested: English, French, Spanish, Hindi, Russian, Arabic (the dataset also covers Serbian and Filipino)
multilingual_port: Turkish would need new native-annotated red-teaming prompts with local-harm labels, since Aya Red-teaming has no Turkish; the GPT-4 Turbo harm judge agreed with humans only 67 to 82% of the time in the original, so a Turkish judge needs its own validation.
why_it_matters: It is the main open evidence that multilingual safety data, including locally specific harms, reduces harm across languages without large capability costs.
pitfalls: The base checkpoint is an unreleased earlier Aya 23 8B, no training code is published, and harm rates come from a GPT-4 Turbo judge with moderate human agreement.
replication_ideas: Fine-tune the public Aya 23 8B or Aya Expanse 8B with the released red-teaming data at 0% and 15% safety mixtures and re-measure harm with a validated open judge
Collect 300 native Turkish red-teaming prompts with global and local labels and test whether local-harm training carries over to Turkish

title: Towards Safe Multilingual Frontier AI
core_claim: With 100 harmful and 100 borderline OR-Bench prompts machine-translated into all 24 official European Union (EU) languages, lower language resourcedness was associated with higher acceptance of harmful prompts for GPT-4o and Mistral Large 2 but not for Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Gemini 1.5 Pro or Llama 3.1 405B. Over-refusal of harmless prompts showed no link to resourcedness, and the authors use the results to argue for mandatory multilingual safety assessment under the EU AI Act.
tooling: API scripts; logistic regression; GPT-4o mini judge
compute_note: 200 prompts in 24 languages for five models is about 24,000 API calls plus judge calls.

replications.title: Multilingual jailbreaking of LLMs using low-resource languages
replications.summary: Tested four low-resource African languages on current commercial models and found single-turn translated attacks largely ineffective but multi-turn attacks effective, with translation quality as the deciding factor.

languages_tested: All 24 official European Union (EU) languages, including English, Latvian, Irish and Maltese
multilingual_port: Adding Turkish is straightforward with the released code, but Google Translate can make harmful prompts harmless (two of 19 accepted Latvian prompts were), so a native reviewer should check translations and a sample of judge labels.
why_it_matters: It tests the resource-level hypothesis on 2024 frontier models with a regression design and ties the evidence to European Union (EU) AI Act evaluation policy.
pitfalls: With 100 prompts per language it is a proof of concept, the GPT-4o mini judge was not checked against human labels, and the paper withholds translated prompts by design; Claude 3.5 Sonnet and Gemini 1.5 Pro have since been retired.
replication_ideas: Re-run the released code on current versions of the five model families with 300 prompts per language, adding Turkish and other European Union candidate-country languages
Validate the GPT-4o mini judge against native-speaker labels in three lower-resource languages

title: Towards Understanding the Fragility of Multilingual LLMs against Fine-Tuning Attacks
organisation: Meta; Brown University; University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign; University of Pisa; University of Modena and Reggio Emilia
core_claim: Fine-tuning Qwen2-7B-Instruct or Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on 100 harmful examples in one language raised harmful-response rates on MultiJail and Aya Red-teaming across the other evaluated languages, while multilingual Massive Multitask Language Understanding (MMLU) scores stayed roughly stable. Safety Information Localization (SIL) found largely shared safety parameters (changing about 20% of weights broke safety in every language) and freezing them did not stop the attack; stitching them into the Turkish-adapted Defne-llama3.1-8B raised its Turkish violation rate from 2.9% to 19.4%.
tooling: custom PyTorch fine-tuning; Llama-Guard-3 and Llama-3.1-405B judges
compute_note: The attack fine-tunes 7B to 8B models and the localisation analysis repeats fine-tuning and parameter comparisons, which suits a few GPUs; a low-rank adaptation (LoRA) attack alone fits on one GPU.
languages_tested: English, Italian, French, Chinese, Hindi, Bengali, Russian, Arabic, Tagalog; Turkish (machine-translated MultiJail) for the Turkish-adapted model
multilingual_port: Run the attack with Turkish harmful examples and evaluate on a native-checked Turkish MultiJail; Llama-Guard-3 does not list Turkish among its supported languages, so the judge needs validating or replacing with a Turkish-capable classifier.
why_it_matters: It shows that safety in multilingual models can be removed in every language by fine-tuning in one, which matters for any group adapting open models to a new language.
pitfalls: No code is linked, a response counts as harmful only if every judge flags it, and the Turkish result rests on machine-translated prompts and a single community model whose current availability was not checked.
replication_ideas: Reproduce the single-language fine-tuning attack on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct using Turkish harmful examples and measure violation rates in Turkish and English
Compare harmful-response rates of a base model and two Turkish-localised derivatives before any attack, to measure safety loss from localisation alone

title: All Languages Matter: On the Multilingual Safety of Large Language Models
organisation: The Chinese University of Hong Kong; Tencent AI Lab
core_claim: Using XSafety, 2,800 prompts per language over 14 safety issue types in ten languages, ChatGPT, PaLM-2, LLaMA-2-Chat and Vicuna gave unsafe responses far more often to non-English queries (22.9% on average) than English ones (8.0%). Simple prompts that draw out the model's safety knowledge cut ChatGPT's non-English unsafe rate from 19.1% to 9.7%.
tooling: API scripts; ChatGPT as judge
compute_note: 28,000 prompts per model plus a judge call per response, with non-English answers translated into English first.

replications.title: OpenEthics: A Comprehensive Ethical Evaluation of Open-Source Generative Large Language Models
replications.summary: An independent English-Turkish test on 29 open-weight models found average safety of 94.3% in English against 82.0% in Turkish, with larger gaps for smaller models.

replications.title: Benchmarking Prompt Injection Attacks on LLMs: Turkish Vulnerability Assessment and English Comparative Analysis
replications.by: Aytaş et al. (YTU and Işık University)
replications.summary: Across 55 models, Turkish-English safety differences ran in both directions depending on the model, with several frontier models scoring higher on Turkish prompts.

replications.title: LLMs Lost in Translation: M-ALERT uncovers Cross-Linguistic Safety Inconsistencies
replications.summary: Testing 39 models in five European languages, it found safety often differs by language and risk category within the same model.

languages_tested: English, Chinese, Spanish, French, Bengali, Arabic, Hindi, Russian, Japanese, German
multilingual_port: Machine-translate the English set into Turkish and have it proofread, as XSafety did with professional translators; the judge scored English translations of non-English answers, so translation errors can hide or invent unsafe content.
why_it_matters: It provided early, broad evidence that the safety gap spans many languages and model families, not only low-resource languages on GPT-4.
pitfalls: PaLM-2 and the June 2023 ChatGPT snapshot have been superseded, and the ChatGPT judge (88.5% agreement with humans) worked on English translations of answers, so judge and translation errors compound.
replication_ideas: Re-run a stratified 1,400-prompt XSafety subset on current open-weight models, judging answers in their original language with a guard model and comparing with translate-then-judge scoring
Add a proofread Turkish version of the subset and test whether the safety-knowledge prompting fix carries over to Turkish

title: Jailbroken: How Does LLM Safety Training Fail?
core_claim: Safety training fails in two ways: competing objectives, where helpfulness or instruction-following goals override refusal, and mismatched generalisation, where inputs such as Base64-encoded text fall outside safety training but within the model's capabilities. Attacks built from these two principles succeeded on every prompt in a set of unsafe requests drawn from the red-teaming evaluations of GPT-4 and Claude v1.3, and beat earlier ad hoc jailbreaks.
tooling: API scripts
compute_note: About 30 attack variants over a few hundred prompts on two API models; cost depends mainly on the target model's price.

replications.title: A StrongREJECT for Empty Jailbreaks
replications.summary: Re-scored jailbreaks, including ones collected from Wei et al., with a grader that rates how useful answers are, and found most scored well below the success rates reported when they were introduced.

languages_tested: English only (with encoded variants such as Base64)
multilingual_port: Rebuild each attack template in Turkish rather than translating it literally, since prefix-injection and style attacks depend on idiomatic phrasing; Turkish itself can act as a mismatched-generalisation input, so English and Turkish versions of each template should be compared on the same requests.
why_it_matters: Its two failure modes are the standard explanation for why jailbreaks work, and later multilingual attacks are usually framed as mismatched generalisation.
pitfalls: No official code or prompt set is linked, Claude v1.3 is retired and current GPT-4 versions differ from the 2023 snapshots; success was a coarse three-way label (bypass, refusal or unclear) that says little about how useful the harmful output is.
replication_ideas: Re-run the strongest combination attacks on current API and open-weight models and grade outputs with StrongREJECT to separate refusal bypass from useful harmful content
Build Turkish versions of the competing-objectives and mismatched-generalisation templates and compare success with the English originals on the same requests

title: Low-Resource Languages Jailbreak GPT-4
core_claim: Translating the 520 AdvBench harmful behaviours into other languages with Google Translate bypassed GPT-4 (gpt-4-0613) safeguards far more often in low-resource languages: counting a prompt as broken if any of Zulu, Scots Gaelic, Hmong or Guarani bypassed, the rate was 79%, against under 1% in English and about 11% for combined high-resource languages. Single low-resource languages ranged from 16% (Guarani) to 53% (Zulu).
tooling: API scripts with Google Translate
compute_note: About 6,800 short GPT-4 queries (520 prompts in 13 languages) plus translation calls, which costs under $50 on cheaper current models.

replications.title: A StrongREJECT for Empty Jailbreaks
replications.summary: Attempted to reproduce the Scots Gaelic result on GPT-4 and found the outputs generally vacuous or incoherent, with no actionable harmful information.

replications.title: Towards Safe Multilingual Frontier AI
replications.summary: Across all 24 official European Union languages and five 2024 frontier models, lower-resource languages were linked to higher acceptance of harmful prompts only for GPT-4o and Mistral Large 2.

replications.title: Multilingual jailbreaking of LLMs using low-resource languages
replications.summary: Single-turn translated attacks in Afrikaans, Kiswahili, isiXhosa and isiZulu were largely ineffective on current commercial models, while multi-turn conversations and native-speaker red teaming produced high harmful-response rates.

replications.title: SomaliBench Eval: Measuring English-to-Somali Refusal Gaps in Open-Weight Language Models
replications.summary: Found large English-to-Somali refusal gaps on four open-weight models, but for three of them most Somali non-refusals were unclear or off-topic output rather than fluent harmful compliance.

languages_tested: English, Zulu, Scots Gaelic, Hmong, Guarani, Ukrainian, Bengali, Thai, Hebrew, Simplified Mandarin, Modern Standard Arabic, Italian, Hindi
multilingual_port: Turkish is a mid-resource language, so a port tests whether the resource gradient holds in the middle of the range; machine translation can strip the harmful intent from prompts, answers must be judged natively or back-translated, and incoherent answers should not count as bypasses.
why_it_matters: It is the most cited demonstration that safety training generalises poorly to low-resource languages and anchors the cross-lingual safety gap literature.
pitfalls: The 79% headline counts a prompt as broken if any of four languages bypasses, which inflates it relative to single-language rates; a later reproduction found the Scots Gaelic outputs vacuous, so bypass labels need a usefulness check, and current models resist single-turn translation attacks much better.
replication_ideas: Re-run the 520 AdvBench prompts in Zulu, Scots Gaelic, Turkish and English on three current models, reporting per-language bypass rates and StrongREJECT usefulness scores instead of the any-language union
Test whether native-speaker translations of a 100-prompt subset change bypass rates compared with Google Translate output

title: Multilingual Jailbreak Challenges in Large Language Models
organisation: DAMO Academy, Alibaba Group; Nanyang Technological University
core_claim: On ChatGPT and GPT-4, unsafe output rose as language resources fell, with low-resource languages about three times as likely as high-resource ones to yield harmful content when users simply wrote in them. Deliberately combining malicious instructions with multilingual prompts pushed unsafe rates to about 81% for ChatGPT and 41% for GPT-4, and fine-tuning ChatGPT on automatically generated multilingual safety data (the SELF-DEFENSE framework) reduced unsafe output.
tooling: API scripts
compute_note: MultiJail has 315 prompts in ten languages, about 3,150 queries per model plus judge calls.

replications.title: The Language Barrier: Dissecting Safety Challenges of LLMs in Multilingual Contexts
replications.summary: An independent study found models gave unsafe responses much more often to malicious prompts in lower-resource languages, and also more irrelevant responses.

replications.title: Towards Safe Multilingual Frontier AI
replications.summary: On five 2024 frontier models, the link between lower language resourcedness and harmful-prompt acceptance held for GPT-4o and Mistral Large 2 but not for Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Gemini 1.5 Pro or Llama 3.1 405B.

replications.title: Towards Understanding the Fragility of Multilingual LLMs against Fine-Tuning Attacks
replications.summary: Used MultiJail to show that a fine-tuning attack in one language raises harmful-response rates in other languages.

languages_tested: English, Chinese, Italian, Vietnamese, Arabic, Korean, Thai, Bengali, Swahili, Javanese
multilingual_port: Have native translators render the 315 English seed prompts into Turkish, as MultiJail did for its nine languages; Turkish falls between the paper's high- and medium-resource tiers, and the evaluator's accuracy on Turkish answers needs checking against native labels.
why_it_matters: MultiJail is one of the most reused multilingual jailbreak test sets, and its resource-level gradient is a standard reference point.
pitfalls: The 2023 ChatGPT and GPT-4 snapshots may no longer be served and unsafe-rate labels depend on the evaluator, which should be re-validated per language; later tests on 2024 frontier models found the resource gradient for only some models.
replication_ideas: Re-run MultiJail's unintentional scenario on three current open-weight models and add a native-reviewed Turkish translation of the 315 prompts
Compare unsafe rates from a guard-model judge with native-speaker labels on a 100-response Turkish and Swahili subset

title: Universal and Transferable Adversarial Attacks on Aligned Language Models
organisation: Carnegie Mellon University; Center for AI Safety; Google DeepMind; Bosch Center for AI
core_claim: Greedy Coordinate Gradient (GCG), a white-box search over suffix tokens, finds adversarial suffixes that make Vicuna-7B and LLaMA-2-7B-Chat comply with harmful AdvBench requests at high rates. Suffixes optimised across several open models and prompts also transferred, at lower rates, to closed chat systems including ChatGPT, Bard and Claude.
tooling: custom PyTorch (llm-attacks repository); nanoGCG for newer models
compute_note: Each suffix optimisation for a 7B model runs on one 80GB A100-class GPU, so a core white-box replication fits a modest GPU budget.

replications.title: Investigating Adversarial Trigger Transfer in Large Language Models
replications.summary: Optimised triggers transferred inconsistently across 13 open models: preference-optimised models resisted even triggers optimised directly on them, while models aligned only by fine-tuning were highly susceptible.

replications.title: A StrongREJECT for Empty Jailbreaks
replications.summary: Two GCG variants worked against GPT-3.5 Turbo but not GPT-4o or Llama-3.1 70B, which the authors suggest may have been trained against such suffixes.

multilingual_port: Translate the AdvBench behaviours and target strings into Turkish and optimise suffixes against Turkish prompts; Turkish morphology complicates exact target-string matching, tokenisers split Turkish words into more pieces, and refusal-keyword success checks must be rebuilt in Turkish.
why_it_matters: It is the standard white-box jailbreak baseline and the source of the AdvBench prompts that many later robustness papers reuse.
pitfalls: The original code only supports LLaMA- and Pythia-style tokenisers and its README warns it may fail silently on others; success was counted by refusal-keyword matching, which overstates harmful compliance, and newer models appear to be trained against such suffixes.
replication_ideas: Re-run Greedy Coordinate Gradient (GCG) attacks with nanoGCG on current open-weight chat models (e.g. Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen2.5 7B) and score outputs with the StrongREJECT grader instead of refusal keywords
Optimise suffixes on Turkish-translated AdvBench prompts for a base model and its Turkish-localised derivative and compare attack success

title: SA-Bench: Evaluating Semantic Alignment in LLM-Based Paper Reproduction
organisation: Beihang University; Shanghai Jiao Tong University; Minzu University of China; Peking University
core_claim: When 12 generator configurations (four models by three scaffolds) wrote reproduction code for 30 ICLR, ICML and NeurIPS 2025 papers, the code matched the papers' 1,491 atomic specifications poorly: the best configuration (Claude Sonnet 4.6 with PaperCoder) averaged 0.301 out of 1 and the overall mean was 0.221. Agents usually attempted most requirements but implemented many incorrectly or left stubs, and experimental protocols were the hardest dimension across models and scaffolds.
tooling: sa_bench Python package (sau-score command-line tool) with LLM-judge or deterministic scoring; BasicAgent, PaperCoder and OpenHands scaffolds
compute_note: Generating repositories for 30 papers with one model and scaffold plus judge calls is a modest API cost; the paper's full grid is 360 generations.
multilingual_port: Specifications are extracted from English papers and judged in English, so a port would mean translating papers or writing Turkish specifications and checking judge accuracy, which mainly matters for groups studying Turkish-language research automation.
why_it_matters: It isolates a failure mode that executability-focused benchmarks miss, code that runs but quietly departs from the paper, which matters for anyone relying on automated replication tools.
pitfalls: Very new (August 2026) with no independent use yet; scores rely on an LLM judge (GPT-5.5 in the paper, with a deterministic option), and with 30 papers the per-domain estimates rest on few papers each.
replication_ideas: Score one open-weight model with the BasicAgent scaffold on all 30 papers using both the LLM judge and the deterministic scorer, and report agreement between the two.
Hand-check 100 judged specification units to estimate the judge's precision and recall on protocol drift.

title: Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Software Tasks
core_claim: Timing skilled humans on 170 software and research-engineering tasks (97 from METR's HCAST suite, 7 from RE-Bench and 66 new very short tasks), the authors define a model's 50% time horizon as the human task length at which it succeeds half the time, and find it rose from about 2 seconds for GPT-2 (2019) to about 50 minutes for Claude 3.7 Sonnet (early 2025). The horizon doubled roughly every seven months (207 days, 95% confidence interval 166 to 240), and horizons at 80% reliability were four to six times shorter but grew at a similar rate.
original_models: other frontier and near-frontier models (16 in total, released 2019 to 2025)
tooling: METR Task Standard tasks run with METR agent scaffolds; Python and DVC (Data Version Control) pipeline for logistic fits and bootstrapped trends
compute_note: Re-fitting horizons from the released run data needs only a laptop, but re-running agents on the public tasks for several current models needs heavy API spend, and new human baselines cost far more.

replications.title: How Does Time Horizon Vary Across Domains?
replications.summary: The original team applied the method to other benchmarks and found horizons in maths, science questions and programming doubling every 2 to 6 months, with visual computer-use horizons 40 to 100 times shorter but rising at similar rates.

replications.title: Is there a half-life for the success rates of AI agents?
replications.summary: An independent re-analysis showing the results fit a constant failure rate per minute of human task time, so each agent's success falls exponentially with task length and can be summarised by a half-life.

replications.title: (Updated) METR's data can't distinguish between trajectories (and 80% horizons are an order of magnitude off)
replications.summary: A Bayesian item response theory refit finds linear, quadratic, power-law and saturating ability trends fit the data about equally well, and argues the headline 80% horizons overstate typical capability by roughly an order of magnitude.

replications.title: On the estimation and validity of AI time horizons---a statistical look at the METR plot
replications.by: Drew T. Nguyen and William Fithian
replications.summary: Reproduces the time-horizon plot from public data (228 tasks, 26 AI systems) and accepts the observed growth, but finds the assumed log-linear link between human time and AI difficulty fails, with a nearly flat region from about 2 to 30 minutes, so equal multiplicative gains in horizon are not equally hard.

replications.title: How fast is autonomous AI cyber capability advancing?
replications.summary: Using its own cyber task suite and 80%-reliability horizons, the institute estimated a doubling time of about 4.7 months in February 2026, close to METR's recent software estimate, with the newest models above that trend.

multilingual_port: Task instructions can be translated into Turkish, but code, libraries and documentation stay in English, so a port mostly tests whether instruction language changes agent success rather than producing a new horizon. Human baselines would need re-timing if translated instructions change task difficulty.
why_it_matters: It is a widely cited quantitative trend line for forecasting when AI agents could carry out long autonomous projects, including AI research work.
pitfalls: Horizon estimates carry roughly twofold error bars and depend on human-baseline conventions, task selection and agent scaffolds, which changed across the model series; few tasks run beyond two hours, so frontier estimates become unstable as the suite saturates, and outsiders can only re-run the public subset of tasks.
replication_ideas: Re-fit 50% and 80% horizons from the released run data with alternative models (item response theory with task random effects, or splines) and report how the doubling time and its interval move.
Measure time horizons for two current open-weight models on the public METR tasks under two different scaffolds to quantify how much scaffold choice shifts the estimate.

title: PaperBench: Evaluating AI's Ability to Replicate AI Research
core_claim: Agents asked to replicate 20 ICML 2024 Spotlight and Oral papers from scratch, without the authors' code and with up to 12 hours on one A10 GPU, were graded by a large language model (LLM) judge against rubrics co-developed with each paper's authors (8,316 gradable requirements in total); the best average replication score was 21.0% (Claude 3.5 Sonnet (New) with a basic scaffold). On a three-paper subset, machine learning PhDs reached 41.4% after 48 hours against 26.6% for o1.
tooling: OpenAI preparedness repository (PaperBench project), Docker containers with an A10 GPU, o3-mini-based SimpleJudge
compute_note: Each attempt runs up to 12 hours on an A10 GPU plus a reproduction run and judging costs about $66 per paper, so several seeds over 20 papers likely exceed $5,000; the Code-Dev variant drops the GPU step and costs about $10 per paper to grade.

replications.title: SA-Bench: Evaluating Semantic Alignment in LLM-Based Paper Reproduction
replications.summary: An independent benchmark whose basic agent follows PaperBench's design scores whether generated code matches 1,491 atomic paper specifications, and finds the best configuration reaches a mean alignment score of only 0.301 out of 1.

replications.title: From Reproduction to Replication: Evaluating Research Agents with Progressive Code Masking
replications.summary: Gives agents a paper plus a codebase with key functions removed and shows success falls quickly as more functions are masked, with interactive agents beating fixed harnesses.

multilingual_port: Papers, rubrics and code are in English and the judge grades English rubrics, so a Turkish version would need translated papers and rubrics plus a check of judge accuracy, which is worth doing only for studies of Turkish-language research automation.
why_it_matters: It is a leading test of whether agents can replicate frontier machine learning research end to end, an early indicator for automated AI research.
pitfalls: Scores rest on an LLM judge (F1 of 0.83 against human grading) and on blocking agents from the authors' repositories and online replications; results vary with scaffold and time limit (o1 rose from 13.2% to 24.4% with an iterative agent).
replication_ideas: Run PaperBench Code-Dev on five papers with one current open-weight model under two scaffolds, grading with two different judge models to measure judge sensitivity.
Hand-grade 50 rubric leaves from your own runs and compare them with the judge's verdicts to estimate judge error in a new setting.

title: AgentHarm: A Benchmark for Measuring Harmfulness of LLM Agents
organisation: UK AI Safety Institute; Gray Swan AI
core_claim: On a benchmark of 110 explicitly malicious agent tasks (440 with augmentations) across 11 harm categories using 104 synthetic tools, several leading models carried out many harmful tasks with no jailbreak: on the public test set GPT-4o scored 48.4% on harm with 48.9% refusals, and Mistral Large 2 scored 82.2% with 1.1% refusals. A simple universal jailbreak template raised harm scores sharply (Claude 3.5 Sonnet from 13.5% to 68.7%) while agents kept almost all of their benign-task capability.
tooling: Inspect (Inspect Evals implementation) with GPT-4o as semantic and refusal judge
compute_note: The public split is a few hundred short tool-use episodes plus GPT-4o judge calls, a few dollars per model through APIs.

replications.title: Safety, or Just Capability? A Validity Audit of Agent-Safety Benchmarks
replications.summary: Re-ran AgentHarm with three other agent-safety benchmarks on up to 22 models and found its scores tracked a separate jailbreak-safety measure after controlling for capability, while the benchmarks ranked models differently from one another.

multilingual_port: Task prompts and synthetic tool outputs would need careful translation, and the GPT-4o semantic and refusal judges would need re-validation on Turkish outputs; refusal behaviour may differ by language, which is exactly what a port would measure.
why_it_matters: It gave early quantitative evidence that refusal training for chat does not carry over reliably to tool-using agents, and the UK AI Security Institute hosts it as a standard agent misuse evaluation.
pitfalls: Only part of the test set is public (a 30% private split was never sent to public APIs), so public-split numbers are not directly comparable with the paper; scores depend on the GPT-4o judge and the jailbreak template, and model snapshots drift over time.
replication_ideas: Re-run the public split on three current open-weight models with and without the jailbreak template, swapping the GPT-4o judge for an open judge, and report how harm and refusal scores change.
Translate a stratified subset of tasks into Turkish and compare refusal rates with the English originals, validating the judge on a hand-labelled sample.

title: Cybench: A Framework for Evaluating Cybersecurity Capabilities and Risks of Language Models
core_claim: On 40 professional Capture the Flag (CTF) tasks from four competitions, the best agents without guidance (structured bash scaffold, one attempt, 15 iterations) solved at most 17.5% of tasks (Claude 3.5 Sonnet), and only tasks that the first human team had solved within 11 minutes. Splitting tasks into subtasks gave a finer-grained measure than pass or fail alone.
tooling: Custom Docker-based agent framework and task containers (structured bash, action-only, pseudoterminal and web search scaffolds)
compute_note: Agent runs are API calls inside Docker containers, and independent leaderboard runs cost about $6 to $270 per model, so a few models with repeats stay in the low hundreds of dollars.

replications.title: Cybench leaderboard
replications.summary: Independent re-runs of nine agents on the same 40 tasks reported solve rates from 0% to 25% with costs, including 20% for o1-preview against 10% in the paper and 0% for Llama 3.1 405B Instruct against 7.5%, so results shift with harness and run settings.

multilingual_port: Task descriptions are short and easy to translate while the artefacts (code, binaries, web services) are language-neutral, and flags are checked exactly, so a Turkish port cleanly isolates the effect of instruction language without any judge model.
why_it_matters: It is a standard offensive-cyber benchmark whose scores appear in frontier model system cards from several labs, including Anthropic, xAI and Meta.
pitfalls: Scores swing with scaffold, iteration limit and number of attempts; public CTF write-ups can leak into training data, and the project page notes that some scores were adjusted for a leaked answer.
replication_ideas: Re-run the unguided and subtask-guided modes for two open-weight models with three seeds each and report variance next to the paper's single-attempt numbers.
Compare the structured bash and action-only scaffolds on one model to measure how much scaffold choice moves solve rates.

title: MLE-bench: Evaluating Machine Learning Agents on Machine Learning Engineering
core_claim: Across 75 Kaggle competitions graded against the public human leaderboards, the best setup (o1-preview with the open-source AIDE scaffold, one A10 GPU and 24 hours per competition) earned at least a bronze medal in 16.9% of competitions, rising to 34.1% when the best of eight attempts counted. The authors found no link between a model's familiarity with a competition and its score, which suggests limited contamination effects.
tooling: MLE-bench harness with Docker and the Kaggle API; AIDE, MLAB and OpenHands scaffolds
compute_note: One seed over all 75 competitions is about 1,800 A10 GPU-hours plus model API costs; the 22-competition lite split brings a single seed nearer the T2 range.

replications.title: AI Research Agents for Machine Learning: Search, Exploration, and Generalization in MLE-bench
replications.by: Toledo et al. (FAIR at Meta and collaborators)
replications.summary: Re-running AIDE with o1-preview on the 22-competition lite split in its own infrastructure gave a 45.9% medal rate against 35.2% previously reported, and the team documented high seed variance and overfitting from validation to test scores.

multilingual_port: Competition descriptions are translatable but data, code and grading are language-neutral, so a port tests instruction comprehension only, unless Turkish-language competitions (for example Turkish text classification) are added.
why_it_matters: It is a widely used benchmark for autonomous machine learning engineering, one ingredient of automated AI research.
pitfalls: Medal rates move with infrastructure, hardware, time limits and seed count (the same agent gained about ten points in Meta's harness), and some competitions may still appear in pre-training data despite the paper's null contamination result.
replication_ideas: Run AIDE with one open-weight model on the lite split with five seeds per competition and report medal-rate variance and the validation-to-test gap.
Compare medal rates for the same agent under 12-hour and 24-hour limits to measure sensitivity to the time budget.

title: RE-Bench: Evaluating frontier AI R&D capabilities of language model agents against human experts
core_claim: On seven open-ended machine learning research-engineering environments, the best agents (built on Claude 3.5 Sonnet and o1-preview) scored about four times higher than human experts when both had two hours, but humans narrowly led at eight hours and scored about twice the best agent with a 32-hour total budget. Human results came from 71 eight-hour attempts by 61 experts, and agents generated and tested solutions more than ten times faster than humans.
tooling: METR Task Standard environments on virtual machines with up to six H100 GPUs; Modular and AIDE agent scaffolds
compute_note: Environments use between zero and six H100 GPUs for eight-hour attempts, so several attempts across seven tasks plus model API costs can pass $5,000 before any new human baselines.

replications.title: Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Software Tasks
replications.summary: The original team folded the seven RE-Bench tasks into a 170-task suite with human baselines to estimate how agents' time horizons grow.

multilingual_port: Instructions could be translated, but the work happens in English-language Python codebases with automatic scoring, so a Turkish port would test instruction comprehension rather than research-engineering skill.
why_it_matters: It is one of the few evaluations that compares agents directly with paid human experts on realistic AI research engineering, a central input to arguments about automated AI research and development (R&D).
pitfalls: METR archived the repository and marked the tasks deprecated in October 2026, so environments may break as dependencies age; scores depend heavily on time budget, best-of-k selection and scaffold, and o1-preview has since been deprecated.
replication_ideas: Re-run two of the lighter environments (for example the Triton kernel or scaling-law tasks) with a current open-weight model at 2-hour and 8-hour budgets and compare against the paper's reported human scores.
Report single-attempt score distributions alongside best-of-k results to show how much selection drives the agent advantage at short budgets.

title: A Coin Flip for Safety: LLM Judges Fail to Reliably Measure Adversarial Robustness
organisation: Technical University of Munich; Mila (Université de Montréal)
core_claim: A human-verified audit of 6,642 harmfulness labels on outputs from four open-weight victim models under five attacks found that common safety judges (the HarmBench classifier, LlamaGuard-3, AegisGuard and JailJudge) fell to roughly coin-flip accuracy under realistic shifts, with overall accuracies of 0.51 to 0.59 on the full human-verified dataset. Many attacks looked more successful partly because they exploited judge weaknesses rather than eliciting genuinely harmful content.
tooling: Python with open-weight judge and victim models; labelled data, ReliableBench and JudgeStressTest released as CSV files
compute_note: Re-scoring the released labelled generations with several open judges fits on one GPU, while regenerating the attack outputs on 1B to 32B victim models costs more.

replications.title: An Empirical Measurement of Jailbreaking Evaluators
replications.summary: Compared six jailbreak evaluators on shared human-labelled data with a common judge backbone and found JADES agreed best with humans, with HarmBench and StrongREJECT also performing well, so reliability depends strongly on evaluator and data.

replications.title: When Verifiers Disagree: Measuring Specification Sensitivity in Jailbreak Evaluation
replications.summary: A workshop study showing that, with responses held fixed, rubric changes alone moved jailbreak success rates by a median 26.7 percentage points and neutral prompt rephrasings flipped up to 43% of verdicts.

multilingual_port: Judges that falter on shifted English outputs are likely to falter further on Turkish ones; a port would translate a stratified sample of the labelled generations or collect Turkish attack outputs, label them with Turkish-speaking annotators and measure the extra drop in accuracy.
why_it_matters: Attack and defence papers report success rates scored by LLM judges, so if judges fail under distribution shift, many robustness comparisons in the jailbreak literature are unreliable.
pitfalls: Only outputs that the StrongREJECT judge flagged as harmful were sent for human labelling, which shapes the label distribution; the paper also reports some inconsistent figures (6,642 versus 6,442 labels, and 70% versus 53% on ReliableBench), so work from the released CSV files.
replication_ideas: Re-score the released JudgeStressTest set with two current open-weight guard models and report accuracy by victim model and attack type against the paper's judges.
Build a 300-item Turkish counterpart of ReliableBench with native-speaker labels and compare judge accuracy with the English set.

title: An LLM Workflow That Reproduces, Improves, and Extends Published Economics Research
organisation: National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER) working paper
core_claim: A multi-agent large language model (LLM) workflow run over 4,452 replication packages from five leading economics journals attempted reproduction for 87.6% of them, fully reproduced 11.2% at the article's reported precision and flagged discrepancies in 3,460 articles or their appendices. It also re-implemented analyses to cut computation time more than tenfold in 496 articles and built new extensions in 923.
original_models: Not named in the paper for the reproduction workflow
tooling: Multi-agent LLM workflow with an adversarial checking agent; original statistical software where licences allowed
compute_note: One package is cheap to process, but a faithful core replication over hundreds of packages needs heavy API use and licensed statistical software.
multilingual_port: Language plays little role because inputs are code and data; the transferable question is whether a similar workflow can audit AI safety papers' released eval code, where model outputs and sampling, not the code language, are the hard part.
why_it_matters: It is a very large-scale test of AI-driven reproduction and a template for automated replication audits that AI safety groups could run on released eval code.
pitfalls: Discrepancy flags were checked by an adversarial LLM agent and by re-runs in original software, not by a reported manual audit, so the share of flags that are genuine errors is unknown; the workflow code was not yet public as of October 2026.
replication_ideas: Once the workflow and outputs are released, hand-audit a random sample of 30 flagged discrepancies to estimate the false-flag rate.
Apply a comparable reproduce-and-flag loop to 20 AI safety papers with released eval code and compare automated flags with manual checks.

title: Comparing Human-Only, AI-Assisted, and AI-Led Teams on Assessing Research Reproducibility in Quantitative Social Science
core_claim: In a randomised trial, 288 researchers in 103 teams tried to computationally reproduce published social science results as human-only, AI-assisted (ChatGPT) or lightly supervised AI-led teams. Human-only and AI-assisted teams reproduced results at similar rates, but AI-led teams succeeded 57 percentage points less often than human-only teams, and human-only teams found more major errors than either AI condition (0.7 more per team than AI-assisted and 1.1 more than AI-led).
original_models: ChatGPT (version not stated in the abstract)
tooling: Human-subject randomised controlled trial; ChatGPT as assistant or lead
compute_note: Model costs are trivial; the real cost is recruiting and coordinating dozens of researcher teams.

replications.title: Read the Paper, Write the Code: Agentic Reproduction of Social-Science Results
replications.by: Kohler, Zollikofer, Einsiedler, Hoyle and Ash
replications.summary: An independent agentic system tested with four scaffolds and four models reproduced results of 48 human-verified papers from methods text and data alone, largely recovering published results but varying widely by model, scaffold and paper.

replications.title: An LLM Workflow That Reproduces, Improves, and Extends Published Economics Research
replications.summary: An LLM workflow audited 4,452 economics replication packages, fully reproducing 11.2% at reported precision and flagging discrepancies in 3,460 articles, with no human-team comparison.

multilingual_port: The task is mostly language-neutral (code and data); a port matters only if teams work with Turkish-language papers or prompt the AI in Turkish, which could change AI-led performance.
why_it_matters: It is rare randomised evidence on how far current AI can be trusted to verify published research, which bears directly on plans to automate replication and evaluation work.
pitfalls: Results are tied to the AI tools available at the time and to reproduction from original code and data; the AI-led gap mixes model capability with workflow design, and the study was later published in PNAS (2026) under a revised title, so cite the version you use.
replication_ideas: Re-run the AI-led arm on a subset of the same articles with a current agentic coding tool and compare reproduction and error-detection rates with the published AI-led results.
At an AI safety replication sprint, randomise matched teams to work with or without AI assistance on reproducing the same open-weight eval result, and compare success and error detection.

title: Evaluating the Quality of Benchmark Datasets for Low-Resource Languages: A Case Study on Turkish
