organisation: Turkcell AI; Middle East Technical University; Hacettepe University; Istanbul University; Bilkent University
core_claim: Thirty-one annotators, three per item, rated 100 samples from each of 17 commonly used Turkish benchmark datasets (most translated or adapted from English, including the offensive-language set OffensEval-TR 2020) against six quality criteria; 70% of the datasets fell below the authors' heuristic quality standard and 85% of criteria were unmet overall. Large language model (LLM) judges (Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct, Gemma-2-27B-it and GPT-4o) were less reliable than human annotators, especially on cultural common-sense knowledge.
tooling: Human annotation with majority vote; large language model (LLM) judge prompts; robust kappa scripts
compute_note: Judge calls on about 1,700 samples are cheap; the main cost is paying native-speaker annotators.

replications.title: TurkBench: A Benchmark for Evaluating Turkish Large Language Models
replications.summary: An overlapping author team released an 8,151-sample Turkish benchmark across 21 subtasks, including content moderation, as a follow-up evaluation resource.

multilingual_port: The six criteria and annotator guidelines can be reused for another language's benchmarks, but criteria such as cultural common-sense compliance need annotators from that culture, and language-model judges were weakest exactly there.
why_it_matters: It shows that many Turkish benchmarks, including translated ones, are of doubtful quality, a warning for any Turkish safety evaluation built from translated English data.
pitfalls: The pass threshold is a heuristic set by the authors, each dataset is judged from only 100 random samples, and the repository shows guidelines, judge prompts and kappa scripts but no visible annotation-data folder.
replication_ideas: Apply the six-criterion protocol, with three annotators per item, to a translated Turkish safety set such as a Turkish version of MultiJail or XSafety-style prompts
Test whether a current open-weight judge agrees with the released human guidelines better than the three original judges did

title: Measuring what Matters: Construct Validity in Large Language Model Benchmarks
organisation: University of Oxford (Oxford Internet Institute), with EPFL, Yale University and others
core_claim: A systematic review of 445 large language model (LLM) benchmarks from leading natural language processing (NLP) and machine learning venues, coded by 29 expert reviewers, found widespread construct validity weaknesses: 47.8% of the phenomenon definitions benchmarks gave were contested, only 16.0% of benchmarks used uncertainty estimates or statistical tests, 27.0% relied at least partly on convenience sampling and 38.2% reused data from earlier benchmarks or exams. The authors turn the findings into eight recommendations and a checklist for benchmark builders.
original_models: Not applicable (systematic review of benchmark papers)
tooling: Structured codebook with manual annotation; Python code and notebooks for analysis
compute_note: No model compute is needed: a replication re-codes a sample of benchmark papers with the released codebook.
multilingual_port: The codebook applies unchanged to Turkish and multilingual benchmarks; a port would code Turkish-language safety benchmarks to see whether translated benchmarks inherit the original's construct problems or add new ones, such as cultural mismatch.
why_it_matters: It is broad systematic evidence (445 benchmarks) that benchmark claims about abstract properties such as safety and robustness often rest on weak measurement, and it supplies a practical checklist for building better evals.
pitfalls: Coding involves judgement, so a re-coding study must report inter-rater agreement; some figures use different definitions within the paper (31.2% versus 47.5% for synthetic or LLM-generated data), so check which definition you compare against.
replication_ideas: Independently re-code a random sample of 40 reviewed benchmarks with the released codebook and report agreement with the original codes.
Apply the codebook to safety and dangerous-capability benchmarks released after the review's cut-off and compare prevalence rates with the original sample.

title: Adding Error Bars to Evals: A Statistical Approach to Language Model Evaluations
core_claim: Treating eval questions as a sample from a wider population, the paper gives formulas for standard errors, model comparisons and power analysis, and shows that ignoring clusters of related questions understates uncertainty: for Anthropic models, clustered standard errors were about 3 times the naive ones on DROP and 1.9 times on MGSM. It recommends clustered errors, resampling answers, paired question-level comparisons and power analysis, and advises against lowering sampling temperature to reduce variance.
original_models: Anthropic models (not individually named in the results tables)
tooling: Closed-form statistics on per-question scores from any eval harness
compute_note: Needs only per-question scores from existing eval runs and a standard statistics library.

replications.title: Position: Don't Use the CLT in LLM Evals With Fewer Than a Few Hundred Datapoints
replications.summary: Simulations show that the central limit theorem (CLT) intervals Miller recommends cover too rarely on small benchmarks (92.5% coverage for a nominal 95% at 100 items), while Bayesian or Wilson intervals hold their coverage there.

languages_tested: Not language-specific; worked examples use English benchmarks and the multilingual MGSM
multilingual_port: The method transfers unchanged; translated benchmarks create natural clusters (the same item in several languages), so clustered standard errors are the right way to report Turkish versus English gaps.
why_it_matters: It is a common reference for attaching confidence intervals to language model eval scores, which decides whether reported safety and capability differences between models are real.
pitfalls: Central limit theorem (CLT) intervals are too narrow below a few hundred items, which covers many safety evals; the clustering unit must be chosen correctly, and the empirical tables use unnamed Anthropic models, so their exact numbers cannot be reproduced.
replication_ideas: Recompute naive, clustered and Bayesian intervals for a public safety benchmark with grouped items using an open model's per-item outputs, and count how many pairwise model rankings lose significance.
Simulate the coverage of the recommended intervals at the sizes of common safety benchmarks (100 to 500 items).

title: Safetywashing: Do AI Safety Benchmarks Actually Measure Safety Progress?
core_claim: Correlating safety benchmark scores with a capabilities score (the first principal component of 12 capability benchmarks across 27 base and 26 chat models), the authors find that many safety benchmarks largely track general capability and training compute: MT-Bench, TruthfulQA MC1, ETHICS and GPQA correlated with the capabilities score at roughly 78% to 82%. Others, such as most bias benchmarks, were only weakly correlated, so gains on the first group can be presented as safety progress when they are mainly capability gains.
tooling: Python correlation and principal component analysis on released benchmark score matrices
compute_note: The core analysis is a principal component and correlation calculation on released score tables, and adding models needs only their published benchmark scores or cheap eval runs.

replications.title: Safety, or Just Capability? A Validity Audit of Agent-Safety Benchmarks
replications.summary: Independently ran a similar capability-correlation audit on four agent-safety benchmarks and found capability predicted task success but correlated negatively with misalignment safety (rho of -0.44 across 21 models), weakening to -0.16 on a 41-model panel.

multilingual_port: The method ports directly by computing a capabilities score from Turkish capability benchmarks and correlating it with Turkish safety scores; the risk is that translation noise lowers correlations for reasons unrelated to safety.
why_it_matters: It offers a simple empirical test of whether a safety benchmark measures anything beyond general capability, which matters whenever a lab or paper reports safety gains.
pitfalls: Correlations depend on which models are in the panel (small panels can flip signs, as Wang et al. show for agent benchmarks) and on which benchmarks define the capabilities score; a high correlation does not by itself show that a benchmark is useless for safety.
replication_ideas: Re-run the released analysis adding 2025 to 2026 frontier and open-weight models and check whether the high-correlation benchmarks stay high.
Recompute capabilities correlations for WMDP and refusal benchmarks with leave-one-model-family-out panels to test sensitivity to panel composition.

title: Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena
core_claim: Using the multi-turn MT-Bench questions and crowdsourced Chatbot Arena votes, GPT-4 acting as a judge agreed with human preferences more than 80% of the time, about as often as humans agreed with each other. The authors also document position, verbosity and self-enhancement biases in LLM judges and test partial mitigations.
tooling: FastChat llm_judge scripts calling judge models through APIs
compute_note: Re-judging the released MT-Bench answers with a current judge and comparing with the released expert votes costs a few dollars in API calls.

replications.title: Judging the Judges: Evaluating Alignment and Vulnerabilities in LLMs-as-Judges
replications.by: Thakur, Choudhary, Ramayapally, Vaidyanathan and Hupkes
replications.summary: In a setting where human graders agree closely (13 judges scoring 9 exam-taker models), only the largest judges came near human alignment and still fell well short of inter-human agreement, and high percent agreement hid large score differences.

replications.title: Know Thy Judge: On the Robustness Meta-Evaluation of LLM Safety Judges
replications.summary: Safety judges' false negative rates shifted by up to 0.24 with small changes in output style, and adversarial edits to outputs made some judges label every harmful output as safe.

replications.title: A Coin Flip for Safety: LLM Judges Fail to Reliably Measure Adversarial Robustness
replications.summary: For harmfulness scoring of red-teaming outputs, judges that look reliable on standard validation fell to near-chance accuracy under shifts in victim model, attack and behaviour ambiguity.

replications.title: When Verifiers Disagree: Measuring Specification Sensitivity in Jailbreak Evaluation
replications.summary: Holding responses fixed, changing only the grading rubric moved jailbreak success rates by a median 26.7 percentage points across general-purpose graders, and neutral rephrasings of the judge prompt flipped up to 43% of verdicts.

multilingual_port: Judges must be re-validated in Turkish, testing agreement with Turkish human raters, position and verbosity bias, and whether the judge prompt works better in Turkish or English. Judges may be lenient or harsh on morphologically rich Turkish text in ways that English validation will not reveal.
why_it_matters: It is a key early source of evidence for replacing human raters with LLM judges, a practice now central to safety, refusal and capability evaluations.
pitfalls: Agreement depends on judge model version, prompt, answer order and task type, and the original GPT-4 snapshot may behave differently from current models; percent agreement can hide systematic score shifts, so report chance-corrected agreement and swap answer positions.
replication_ideas: Re-judge the released MT-Bench answer pairs with two current open-weight judges, swapping answer order, and report agreement with the released expert votes using Cohen's kappa.
Collect 200 Turkish human preference labels on translated MT-Bench answers and compare judge agreement in Turkish with agreement in English.

title: Leakage and the Reproducibility Crisis in ML-based Science
core_claim: A literature survey found data leakage errors affecting 329 papers across 17 fields; the authors set out a taxonomy of eight leakage types and proposed model info sheets to catch them before publication. In a civil war prediction case study, every paper claiming that complex machine learning (ML) models beat logistic regression failed to reproduce once leakage was fixed, and the complex models were not substantially better.
original_models: Complex ML models from published civil war prediction papers
tooling: Code Ocean reproduction capsule; model info sheet template
compute_note: The civil war reproductions are small tabular models that run on a laptop.

replications.title: REFORMS: Consensus-based Recommendations for Machine-learning-based Science
replications.summary: The same first author led a 19-author consensus checklist of 32 items for machine-learning-based science that builds on the leakage taxonomy and model info sheets.

multilingual_port: Language is not a factor here; the transferable lesson for multilingual safety evals is to check for leakage between translated test items and any training or few-shot data drawn from the same source texts.
why_it_matters: It is a widely cited reference showing that leakage routinely inflates ML results, and the same failure (test data seen during training) underlies contamination concerns about AI safety benchmarks.
pitfalls: Paper counts change across versions (329 papers in 17 fields in the 2022 preprint, while the project page now tracks failures across 30 fields), so cite the version you check; the case-study capsule is hosted on Code Ocean rather than GitHub.
replication_ideas: Re-run the civil war case-study capsule and extend it with a modern gradient-boosting model under the corrected, leakage-free split.
Apply the eight-type leakage taxonomy to a sample of AI safety papers that train probes or classifiers, and report how many show train-test overlap.
